title: Electron Hydrodynamics and Bernoulli Effect in Venturi-Shaped 2D Systems
authors: C. A. Monari, A. D. Levin, A. S. Jaroshevich, Z. D. Kvon, V. A. Chitta, D. V. Dmitriev, A. K. Bakarov, G. M. Gusev
abstract: The study of electron hydrodynamics provides a powerful framework for understanding transport in ultraclean conductors, yet experimental evidence has thus far been largely restricted to the linear-response regime. Here, we report the direct observation of a strongly nonlinear transport regime in a high-mobility two-dimensional electron system. By engineering devices with a Venturi-shaped wedge geometry specifically designed to enhance convective nonlinearities, we uncover a pronounced nonlinear voltage response and large diodicity in the current-voltage characteristics. Our experimental findings show quantitative agreement with a theoretical model that attributes the observed nonlinearity to the convective acceleration of the electron fluid, analogous to the Bernoulli effect. These results provide compelling evidence for the applicability of the hydrodynamic framework to two-dimensional electron transport and open new avenues for exploring nonlinear and preturbulent phenomena in solid-state systems.
summary: This work reports direct experimental evidence of strongly nonlinear electron transport in 2D conductors by engineering Venturi-shaped devices. The observed large current asymmetry is successfully modeled using an electron hydrodynamic framework, confirming the applicability of fluid dynamics principles (like the Bernoulli effect) to solid-state charge transport.
main_problem: To observe and study strongly nonlinear transport regimes in electron systems beyond the linear response regime, particularly investigating the role of geometry.
main_result: The authors experimentally observed a pronounced nonlinear voltage response and large diode-like asymmetry in Venturi-shaped 2D electron systems, quantitatively agreeing with a hydrodynamic model analogous to the Bernoulli effect.
method: Transport measurements were performed on high-mobility 2D electron systems using devices fabricated with engineered Venturi geometries, measuring differential resistance ($r = dV_{xx}/dI_{	ext{dc}}$) under varying DC bias and temperature.
model_or_system: The study utilizes a viscous hydrodynamic framework to model electron transport in GaAs quantum wells (single-layer and bilayer). The geometry is crucial, as the nonlinearity is enhanced by the Venturi constriction, leading to convective acceleration effects.
key_observables: Nonlinear voltage response, large diode asymmetry in I-V characteristics, differential resistance ($r$) vs. $I_{	ext{dc}}$ and $T$, and the symmetrized current $I_{	ext{sym}}(V_0)$.
important_parameters: Venturi geometry dimensions ($W_{	ext{in}}, W_{	ext{out}}$), temperature ($T$), applied DC current ($I_{	ext{dc}}$), and electron-electron scattering rates.
main_assumptions: The analysis treats geometric parameters as effective estimates, ignoring potential renormalizations from finite slip or edge depletion; the hydrodynamic model is assumed valid when $\ell_{ee} \ll W \ll l$.
figures_summary: Figures show optical images and calculated flow patterns for the Venturi geometry. Subsequent figures track differential resistance vs. DC current and temperature, highlighting the strong asymmetry in the Venturi case compared to symmetric channels.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need to study nonlinear transport beyond linear response. It details measurements on specific geometries (Venturi vs. constant width) to isolate geometric effects. Finally, it compares these findings with a full hydrodynamic model incorporating temperature and magnetic field dependencies.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state transport rather than quantum information, the use of non-equilibrium hydrodynamics to describe electron flow in mesoscopic structures touches upon concepts relevant to open quantum systems where dissipation and geometry dictate dynamics.
